2. Respondent No. 1 as plaintiff instituted the aforesaid Title Suit against the appellant and respondent Nos. 2-5 for declaration of his title to the property in schedule annexed to the plaint and confirmation of possession therein and alternatively recovery of khas possession of the same. The plaint case is that, respondent No. 4 Rabindra Kumar Dey had purchased the suit land from the original owner, the Eastern Commercial Bank Ltd in the benami of his elder brother respondent No. 3 Birendra Kumar Dey who did not pay any consideration, by registered kabala dated 24-8-44 AD as he was indebted to many persons at the relevant time. Rabindra Kumar raised structures and let out the same to monthly tenants. Rabindra paid rents and taxes in the name of his brother Birendra Kumar and after he left this country Rabindra got his own name mutated in the settlement papers and in the municipality and ever since paid rents and taxes in his own name. The Government realised rent from Rabindra who paid up the certificate dues in Certificate Case No. 28330 of 1960-61. Rabindra''s brother Birendra had sworn an affidavit on 7-5-64 before the Presidency Magistrate, Calcutta, declaring that he was simply a benamder of Rabindra Kumar who was the real owner of the property. Rabindra sold the property to respondent No. 1 for a consideration of Rs. 15,000.00 by a registered kabala dated 20-11-63 AD. Respondent No. 1 after purchase mutated his name in the office of the Government and the municipality, and accordingly, paid rent and taxes. Respondent No. 1 filed suits for ejectment of monthy tenants and at this stage, the tenants set up one Asmat Ali who filed an application before the Assistant Custodian of Enemy Property (L&B), Comilla praying for taking lease of the same as enemy property whereupon enemy property Case No. 274 of 1969 was started and after enquiry the Assistant Custodian of Enemy Property by his order dated 21-4-69 held that the suit property was not an enemy property. But subsequently, the tenants of the plaintiff managed to influence the Assistant Custodian and obtained an order dated 5-5-69 behind the back of respondent No. 1 declaring the suit property as enemy property. On coming to know about the aforesaid order respondent No. 1 filed Title Suit No. 263 of 1969 in the Court of Munsif, 3rd Court, Comilla challenging the legality of the order dated 5-5-69 but the suit was withdrawan and Writ Petition No.177 of 1969 was filed for speedy relief. The Rule in the Writ Petition was discharged on 3-6-76 as not maintainable. Thereafter respondent No. 1''s Civil Petition for leave to appeal was also dismissed on 24-11-76. During the pendency of the aforesaid Writ Petition respondent No. 1 instituted the instant suit. 

 4. The Assistant Custodian, defendant-appellant and the said added defendant Abdul Karim contested the suit by filing identical written statements. Their common case is that respondent No. 3 Birendra Kumar was a First Class Contractor and he purchased the suit property with his own fund and owned and possessed the same on payment of rents and taxes in his own name. He left for India in 1958 forever. Respondent No.4 used to pay rent and taxes in his name and realised rents from the tenants on his behalf as care-taker. Taking advantage of the absence of Birendra, Rabindra, respondent No.4 managed to have his name recorded in the settlement records and also got his name mutated in municipal record and thereafter paid rents and taxes in his own name. Rabindra never purchased the suit property in the benami of his brother Birendra and he was not the owner of the property and, as such, by purchase on 22-11-63 from him, the plaintiff did not derive any title to the property and he was also not in possession through tenants as alleged. One Asmat Ali applied on 8-2-69 for taking lease of the property as enemy property but through oversight the said property was released on 11-4-69, where after persons in possession of the property filed a petition for review of the order and the Assistant. Custodian, on consideration of the materials on record, declared the suit property as enemy property by order dated 5-5-69. The plaintiff failed to establish his claim in writ petition and lost upto the Appellate Division. The property has been leased out to different persons including respondent No. 5 and they are possessing as lessee under the Assistant Custodian of Enemy Property. The suit is liable to be discharged. 

 5. The suit was decreed by the trial Court holding that the Government accepted Rabindra as the real owner and recorded his name in the record of rights as early as 1960-61 and realised rent from him amicably and also by issuing certificate case. Rabindra was openly and uninterruptedly exercising all right as the real owner since 1960-61 without any objection or opposition from any quarters and upon holding as aforesaid, the learned Subordinate Judge declared that the suit property is not an enemy property. The trial Court also found that DW 1, the Tahsildar stated in his deposition that the suit land was listed as enemy property in the census list in the year 1967 but he could not produce any paper to prove it. The trial Court further found in respect of the genuineness of the transaction of the plaintiff that it is an admitted fact that he purchased the suit land by registered deed, realised rent, mutated his name in the municipality. His purchase was also proved by PW 2. There is no evidence to believe that the purchase of the plaintiff is a sham and bogus transaction. The tenants who admitted him as landlord are no more possessing the suit land in the capacity of tenants but as lessees of the Government. 

 16. It is on record that Birendra Kumar Dey left Bangladesh in 1958 and Rabindra Kumar Dey was staying in Bangladesh. SA Khatian, Ext. 8 was prepared in the year 1960-62 in the name of Rabindra. Municipal assessment holding, Ext. 3 was also made in the name of Rabindra Kumar Dey in the year 1962-63. The receipt of municipal taxes, Ext. 4 series show that taxes were paid by Rabindra Kumar Dey in the year 1962-63, Exts. 5-5A, rent receipts show payment of rent by vendor. Rabindra Kumar Dey after preparation of SA Khatian, Ext. 8. The learned Single Judge found that these documents are all prior to 1965 before the Indo-Pak War and before anybody''s contemplation of coming into force of the Enemy Property Law in this country. The learned Single Judge further found from Ext. 6, that defendant No. 5 (appellant in Civil Appeal No. 23 of 1997) paid rent to Birendra Kumar Dey as monthly tenant. Thereafter he paid rent to Rabindra Kumar Dey and his father. Thus, the learned Single Judge found that defendant No. 5 was aware that Rabindra Kumar Dey was the real owner and to him he was paying rent. It is also on record that defendant No. 5 was paying rent to the plaintiff admitting him as owner after his purchase from Rabindra Kumar Dey. Ext. 7 to 7 (f) are the agreements of the tenants with the plaintiff" as the landlord. Ext 10 also showed that other tenants filed petition admitting that they were tenants under defendant No. 4. Defendant No. 5 also admitted in his cross-examination that he paid rent to the plaintiff. Ext. 10 showed that other tenants filed petition admitting that they were tenants under defendant No. 4 and they never denied that the plaintiff''s vendor was not the real owner. The rent-receipts and tax receipts submitted by the plaintiff were found by the appellate Court to have been initially paid in the name of defendant No. 3 who was, in fact, the benamder and subsequently all these documents were corrected in the name of defendant No. 4, the real owner. 

 19. In the case of Hasan Ali Mollah vs. Jonendra Mohan Biswas, 1984 BLD (AD) 307 it has been held that the question of actual possession or receipt of the rents is one of the most important evidence of benami transaction. In the present case it is on record that Rabindra Kumar Dey was in possession of the land and his brother left the country in 1958. Rabindra Kumar Dey himself was possessing through various tenants. The tenants also admitted that they paid rents to Rabindra Kumar Dey and subsequently to the plaintiff. In the present case, the plaintiff had successfully proved that the purchase money was given by Rabindra Kumar Dey who also possessed the property and the relationship between the parties are that of full brothers and the conduct of Rabindra Kumar Dey in dealing with the property and subsequent sale is evidence of the fact that Rabindra Kumar Dey was the real owner and his brother was only a name-lender. Mr Khandker Mahbubuddin Ahmed, learned Advocate for the respondent, also brought to our notice that the property was purchased in the benami from Commercial Bank, Comilla and for the purchase admittedly payments were made in installment and in such a case it is indeed difficult to bring evidence of actual payment of money when the transaction was with a bank. The learned Single Judge rightly determined the effect of benami transaction from all the documents and surrounding facts and circumstances. 

 20. The defendants adduced two witnesses, namely, DW 1 Tahsilder and DW 2 Abdul Karim (defendant No. 5), a lessee under the vested property authority. DW 1 testified that in the census list of 1967 the disputed property was enlisted as enemy property but he could not produce any paper. He joined office in 1976 for the first time and he only deposed that SA Khatian which was prepared in 1961-62 was wrong. DW 2 Abdul Karim said in his cross-examination that he paid rents to Barindra but he could not produce any rent receipts on the plea that those were burnt. He admitted that on his application Government has granted lease to him and before that he used to pay rent to the plaintiff. This is all the oral evidence on record on behalf of the defendants. 

 21. It is on record that Certificate Case No. 28330/1960-61 was started against defendant No. 4 Rabindra Kumar Dey and the rent was realised from him by the Government as he was in possession and the Government also treated him as the owner of the land. It is also on record that the tenants recognized Rabindra Kumar Dey as the real owner and paid rents to him. The tenants also paid rent to the plaintiff but subsequently they filed an application to treat the property as enemy property as the plaintiff wanted to enhance the rent. It is on the application of the tenants that the Assistant Custodian treated the property of the plaintiff as enemy property and subsequently released the same on 11-4-69 as its inclusion was wrong. It is also found from the record that the order dated 114-69 was passed on the basis of a report submitted by Tahsilder. The Assistant Custodian, Enemy property again reviewed his earlier order and included the property as an enemy property on 5-5-69 without serving any notice to the plaintiff-owner of the property. Such inclusion without serving any notice to the plaintiff when he acquired a vested right is illegal. It was the tenants who were instrumental in listing the property as enemy property. 

 23. In the present case, proforma defendant No. 3 had already left for India in 1958 and Rabindra Kumar Dey sold the property to the plaintiff on 22-11-1963 and to prove the same along with other evidences the plaintiff has also produced Ext. 9, affidavit sworn by Birendra Kumar Dey before the Presidency Magistrate''s Court, Calcutta acknowledging that defendant No. 4 Rabindra Kumar Dey was the real owner and that he was merely a benamder. This exhibit is an important piece of evidence. The lower appellate Court did not consider this document on the ground that the document was inadmissible as it did not come through diplomatic channel and did not contain any notary certificate. The learned Single Judge found that the affidavit sworn outside Bangladesh needed to be notarised by our Embassy or High Commissioner abroad. It appears that Ext. 9 was admitted as exhibit without any objection from the defendants. The learned Single Judge found that no objection having been taken as to the admissibility of the said affidavit on the ground that it was not notarized and certified by the Embassy of Bangladesh on any ground, Ext. 9 was properly and legally admitted in evidence. The learned Single Judge thus correctly found that the appellate Court thus comitted an error of law in holding that Ext. 9 was prima fade inadmissible in evidence. In the case of Abdullah and 3 others vs. Abdul Karim and another 22 DLR 205 it has been held that the objection as to formal proof of a document has to be taken at the earliest point of time and it cannot be taken subsequently and suddenly put in appeal. It was further held in that decision that if a document has been marked as exhibit without objection it becomes admissible in evidence and it should be taken into consideration. The learned Single Judge has rightly considered Ext. 9 as a vital piece of evidence to show that Birendra Kumar Dey, full brother of Rabindra Kumar Dey, clearly stated that the property belonged to his brother and he paid consideration for the same. It cannot be argued that affidavit by itself is an inadmissible piece of document. The affidavit has been sworn before a Magistrate in accordance with law. There may be some omissions as to the fact that it was not duly stamped and it contained no notarized certificate. But these are matters of formal nature and at the trial no objection was taken with regard to these formalities. In such view of the matter we are of the view that the learned Single Judge was correct in holding that non-consideration of this vital document has resulted in a serious failure of justice. In the case of Joynal Abedin and others vs. Mafizur Rahman and others, 44 DLR (AD) 162, it has been held by this Division that a document having been filed and marked as exhibit without any objection the question of inadmissibility of that document cannot be raised at a subsequent point of time and the courts below acted wrongly in not considering that document and the same has materially affected the decision in that case.
